title: Transcription firm Tigerfish exposed customer audio, video and invoices in an open cloud bucket
date_note: Date of TechCrunch's report; the researcher says he found the bucket in October. The exposure date is not stated.
summary: TechCrunch reports that San Francisco-based transcription company Tigerfish, which serves law enforcement, government departments and tech companies, left an Amazon S3 bucket open to anyone with no password. It held police interview transcriptions, body-cam footage, customers' raw audio and video, and invoices. Tigerfish's president told TechCrunch the company has blocked all public access. TechCrunch says it is unclear whether customers were notified.
plain: A transcription company used by police and prosecutors left a cloud storage folder open to anyone online. The company says it has now blocked public access.
exec: Customer recordings and invoices of police and government clients sat in an open cloud bucket; a basic misconfiguration with possible trust and contract consequences.
action: Tigerfish customers should ask the company what data was exposed and for how long; all organisations should check that their cloud storage buckets block public access and directory listing.
impact: Police interview transcriptions, body-cam footage, raw customer audio and video, and invoices were openly accessible; no counts were given.

validation.note: TechCrunch exclusive; it verified the data and the company's president confirmed blocking public access. No second publisher yet.
